“Souper” paper dress

A promotional paper dress from Campbell’s Soup, printed with rows of soup-can labels after Andy Warhol’s Campbell’s Soup Cans.

Source
V&A: Paper dress, T.66-2016
Creator
Campbell’s Soup Inc. (producer)
Made
1967
Style
Pop art (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Commercial, playful, ironic
Evidence
Downloaded and inspected the V&A image of its copy, T.66-2016 (1200 × 1600 px), in a scratchpad. No image is stored.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

The V&A describes a short sleeveless dress of bonded-fibre “paper”, made in the USA in 1967 and produced to promote Campbell’s vegetable soup, after Andy Warhol’s soup cans of 1962. V&A.

The V&A notes that paper dresses were a brief sensation from 1966 to 1968, and that many were free gifts that promoted consumer products. V&A.

The painting series it follows is Campbell’s Soup Cans.

Observed

  • The dress is printed with four rows of soup-can labels in a regular grid; the labels are cut off at the side seams.
  • Each label has a red top half with the white script “Campbell’s” and a white bottom half with “SOUP” in black slab-serif capitals.
  • A gold medallion sits on the line between red and white; a row of small gold fleurs-de-lis runs along the bottom of each label.
  • Thin black vertical lines separate the labels.
  • Two gold stripes run along the hem. The neckline and armholes are bound in black.

Why it belongs

The dress closes the loop between packaging and Pop: a painter’s grid of labels becomes a product’s own promotion.

Repetition of one unit in a strict grid is a Pop layout device as important as the comic panel.

Borrow

Repeat one product unit in a strict grid of cells separated by thin black rules.

Crop the grid at the edges of the container so that it reads as an endless pattern.
